name: Karl Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and isn't linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I make production music, which is the background stuff you hear under podcasts, cooking videos and YouTube adverts. I write it in my bedroom on a laptop and two old synths, then upload it to an online music library that licenses it out and gives me a cut. Most days I'm finishing two or three short tracks, labelled things like 'hopeful tech corporate'. Thursday evenings I rehearse with Glasshouse, an indie band where I play keys, and we gig about twice a month.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI in that work right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use it to name and tag tracks, write the descriptions, sometimes to sketch a chord idea when I'm stuck, and it's sped me up a lot. I'm not a great player, I'm self-taught, so the tools fill gaps. My boyfriend Tomas works as a software tester and teases me that I'm automating myself. He might be right. I've got about five months of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say great, the tools stay useful and nobody's job gets wiped out. I'd probably post a little thread about how I use AI to speed up tagging. I'd also say the bigger fight is still how little streaming and libraries pay artists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my income was already sliding before any of this. The library is flooded with tracks, so each one earns less every year. Last year my average track made about forty euros over its life, down from sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep making tracks and push my output up with the tools. I'd try to get Glasshouse more paid gigs and maybe sell synth patches online. I'd join a group of library composers who are pushing for better royalty splits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless. Not scared, because nothing big changes, but I can see the line on my income chart pointing down anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if that line keeps going down at the same rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In three years I'd be making half what I make now from the same work. My background music already earns less every year, and that's before any robot composer shows up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Tomas's job feel safer than yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funny enough, no. Software testing is exactly the sort of thing AI already eats. We joke that between us we've picked the two most automatable jobs going. But he's on a salary, so at least there's a monthly number.

say: I'd say the **tools stay useful** and nobody's job gets wiped out.
I'd point out that **libraries and streaming** still pay artists too little.
think: My track earnings were **already falling**, from about sixty euros to forty each.
The library is **flooded** with tracks, so each earns less every year.
do: Use AI tools to raise my **track output** each week.
Sell **synth patches** online and get Glasshouse more paid gigs.
Join a **composers' group** pushing for better royalty splits.
feel: **Restless**, watching his **income line** slide even with no big change.
S0.quote: My background music already earns less every year, and that's before any robot composer shows up.
fieldNote: His income was **already shrinking** from oversupply, so the plateau doesn't rescue him.
He uses AI **daily** and sees it as a gap-filler for weak skills.
He's quick to frame it as a **royalties fight**, true to his progressive views.

steps.text: Use AI tagging tools to upload four tracks a week instead of three
Sell synth patch packs on an online marketplace
Join a library composers' group pushing for fairer royalty splits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the libraries have to label AI tracks and keep a share for humans, or the whole system collapses. I'd say it on composer forums and in a couple of interviews if anyone asked. I'd also say people like me should learn the tools rather than pretend they're not there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, background music is gone as a living for someone at my level. If a client can generate 'hopeful tech corporate' in ten seconds, why license mine? The only question is how fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop relying on the library within a year and pivot. I'd offer custom music to podcast makers, using AI to draft fast and then making it personal, with real calls and edits. I'd also start learning how these music models work so I could get work helping studios use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. I'm the person who said learn the tools, and now the tools are doing my job. There's a bit of excitement too, because I'm better placed than most to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would a month's rent come from if the library money dropped by half?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From custom jobs, I hope, maybe two a month at two hundred each, plus gigs. And from savings for a while. Five months of savings sounds like a lot until your main income is a music library that just discovered it doesn't need composers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big platforms, for training on everyone's music without paying. Not the tech itself, I like the tech. I'd want a law that makes them pay into a fund for musicians.

say: I'd say libraries must **label AI tracks** and keep a share for humans.
I'd tell other composers to **learn the tools** rather than ignore them.
think: **Background music** is finished as a living for someone at my level.
Clients can generate my kind of track in **ten seconds**.
do: Move off the **library** within a year and offer custom podcast music.
Learn how **music models** work to help studios use them.
Run down **savings** to cover rent during the switch.
feel: **Anxious** that his tools are taking his job, with a little **excitement** about switching.
S1.quote: Five months of savings sounds like a lot until your main income is a music library that just discovered it doesn't need composers.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his main income** in this scenario, but feels he can move.
He blames **platforms**, not the technology, and wants a law to pay musicians.
His adaptability shows in a quick **pivot plan** to custom work.

steps.text: Offer custom podcast theme music to ten podcast makers
Take an online course on how AI music models work
Use savings to cover rent while custom work builds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when you need a universal basic income, a regular payment from the state for everyone. Not in ten years, now. I'd be very online about it, and I'd go to every protest with Tomas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I'm out of composing by 2028. Every track I make is screen work, so there's no three-year robot gap for me. Even the keys in Glasshouse is only safe if people still pay for live gigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd cut spending hard, sell the second synth and stop eating out. I'd try to get any job helping companies set up AI music systems, because there'll be a short window where that's paid. I'd play live as much as possible, because a human on a stage is the last bit robots reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Both of us would be in jobs that disappear at the same time, mine and Tomas's. That's the bit that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tomas actually decide in that first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably move in with my sister to save rent, she's got a spare room in the suburbs. My boyfriend Tomas and I would have to move in with my sister, two grown adults in a spare room with a synth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the live playing give you any real hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some. Robots don't arrive until 2031 in this picture, so I'd have three years of gigs, if people come out. I'd want Glasshouse to play every venue that would have us.

say: I'd call for a **universal basic income**, a regular state payment, right now.
I'd go to **protests** with Tomas and be very online about it.
think: All my composing is **screen work**, so I'm out by 2028.
Live keys in Glasshouse are only safe if people still **pay for gigs**.
do: Sell the **second synth** and stop eating out.
Look for short-term work **setting up AI music** systems for companies.
Play **live gigs** as often as possible until robots arrive.
feel: **Alarmed** that both he and Tomas lose their jobs at **the same time**.
S2.quote: My boyfriend Tomas and I would have to move in with my sister, two grown adults in a spare room with a synth.
fieldNote: His **whole household** is exposed, which pushes him from anxious to alarmed.
He clearly separates **screen work** from **live playing** and their different timelines.
Moving in with his **sister** came up fast as the fallback.

steps.text: Sell the second synth and stop eating out
Apply for short contracts setting up AI music systems
Move in with his sister to save rent
Join basic income protests with Tomas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set up a basic income and a fund for creative workers, so let's do it. I'd go to party meetings, not just protests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years buys me three or four of composing work, shrinking, then nothing. The live work could last till 2034. That's enough time to build something else if I start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a short course in audio engineering, so I could work on live shows and installations, hands-on stuff. I'd keep using AI to make my composing faster while it still pays. And I'd push Glasshouse to tour more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a direction. It feels like running for a train I can still catch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hands-on work, when you're the one who loves the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the tools will do the screen part better than me, and I've accepted that. I'd rather be the guy plugging in cables at a festival than the guy whose laptop music got replaced by a better laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your bandmates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To play every gig they can and build a real crowd now. A fanbase that knows your names is worth more than a thousand library tracks. People come to see faces.

say: I'd push for a **basic income** and a fund for creative workers within five years.
I'd go to **party meetings**, not only protests.
think: Composing gives me **three or four years**, shrinking, then nothing.
Live work could last until **2034**, which is time to build something else.
do: Start a short **audio engineering** course for live shows.
Use AI to make composing **faster** while it still pays.
Push Glasshouse to **tour more** and build a real crowd.
feel: **Anxious** but with a direction, like running for a **train** he can catch.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the guy plugging in cables at a festival than the guy whose laptop music got replaced by a better laptop.
fieldNote: He's accepted the **screen work** is lost and plans for **hands-on** work.
He moves from protest to **party politics** when there's more time.
His advice to the band is about building a **fanbase**.

steps.text: Enrol in a short live audio engineering course
Use AI to finish library tracks faster while they still pay
Book a Glasshouse tour of small venues next spring
Attend local party meetings on a creative workers' fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to get this right, so there's no excuse for leaving musicians behind. I'd be on the committee of a composers' union by then, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets me move on properly. Thirty-seven is still young. The library income will be long gone before 2036 anyway, so I'd use the time to build a career that doesn't depend on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly trained in live sound and stage tech over two years. I'd keep using AI for anything that saves time and try to make a small business doing sound for festivals. I'd save more, maybe even put a bit into an index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. It's the same end point, but I'd have a decade to get my feet under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make that business work when robots arrive around 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing, to be honest, unless people still want humans around them at a gig. In 2039 a robot can rig a stage, but a festival crowd still wants to see a person behind the mixing desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the long timeline change your life outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Tomas and I have talked about getting married. With ten years of warning, I'd stop treating every year like the last one and actually plan a wedding.

say: I'd say a decade leaves **no excuse** for leaving musicians behind.
I'd join the committee of a **composers' union**.
think: The **library income** will be gone before 2036 anyway.
Ten years lets me build a career that **doesn't depend** on screen work.
do: Train in **live sound** and stage tech over two years.
Put some savings into an **index fund**.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, with time to get his **feet under** him.
S4.quote: In 2039 a robot can rig a stage, but a festival crowd still wants to see a person behind the mixing desk.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets him plan a **business** and even a **wedding**.
He still expects library money to **vanish** well before AGI.
He doubts his business survives **robots** unless crowds still want people.

steps.text: Train in live sound and stage tech over two years
Register a small festival sound business
Put a monthly amount into an index fund
Plan a wedding with Tomas within five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Tomas and I would lose our jobs at the same time and I'd have no time to retrain. What would help is a basic income, or at least a year of wage support, and a fund paid by AI companies for the musicians they trained on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask whether I'd still make music for free. I would. I just want to know if I'm allowed to make a living from it, or if music goes back to being a hobby for people with money.

headlineQuote: With ten years of warning, I'd stop treating every year like the last one and actually plan a wedding.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old production music composer** who also plays keys in an indie band.
He's self-taught, uses **AI tools daily** and has about five months saved.
His boyfriend Tomas is a **software tester**, so their whole household is exposed to thinking AI.
He's **progressive**, blames platforms rather than the tech, and pushes for a basic income.
He pivots fast towards **live and hands-on** work as soon as screen composing looks finished.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he and Tomas would lose their jobs together.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or at least a year of **wage support**.
A **fund** paid by **AI firms** to musicians whose work trained their models.
